name: Cooling and climate
answer: These measures show how a data center removes heat and what that costs in energy and water. AI racks now run hot enough that liquid cooling has replaced air at the high end, so cooling sets a hard limit on how dense a facility can be.

metrics.line: Continuous inlet-air temperature and relative humidity at the rack face, monitored separately for cold aisles that feed equipment and hot aisles that exhaust it.
metrics.label: Temperature and humidity, hot and cold aisle

metrics.line: Cubic feet per minute delivered through the room or containment system, and the pressure differential that drives it through equipment rather than around it.
metrics.label: Airflow and static pressure

metrics.line: Supply and return temperature and flow rate of the coolant loop, whether direct-to-chip cold plates or immersion baths.
metrics.label: Liquid coolant temperature and flow rate

reading.body:
Cooling is now a density limit, not a comfort setting: AI racks run hot enough that liquid cooling has replaced air at the high end.

The measures split into two regimes. Air cooling is tracked through inlet temperature and humidity at the rack face, kept separately for the cold aisles that feed equipment and the hot aisles that exhaust it, plus airflow in cubic feet per minute and the static pressure that pushes it through equipment rather than around it. Liquid cooling is tracked through the supply and return temperature and flow rate of the coolant loop, whether that is direct-to-chip cold plates or immersion baths. The two sets of numbers describe the same job, moving heat off the silicon, by different means.

For AI specifically, the liquid metrics are the ones that govern how much compute fits in a building. Air can only carry so much heat away from a rack, so once rack power rises past what airflow and static pressure can clear, the coolant loop's temperature and flow rate become the ceiling on density. That makes cooling a constraint on scaling that sits alongside power, not behind it.

What this does not cover is efficiency, cost, or water consumption, which sit in the sibling categories on power efficiency and sustainability. It also gives no thresholds, no target values, and no comparison across facilities, so it defines what is measured rather than what counts as good.
